newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan mulls exchange rate target for currency.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan mulls exchange rate target for currency.

text.p: Kazakhstan is considering shifting the focus of currency policy to an exchange rate target from a monetary one as the oil-rich country readies for a rise in capital inflows, a senior central banker said on Wednesday.
The National Bank of Kazakhstan currently targets money supply growth and exchange rate movements are geared to meeting this goal, deputy chairman Grigory Marchenko said.
"The key issue for the future is whether we keep a monetary anchor or introduce an exchange rate anchor, most probably a crawling peg," he told Reuters.
Under a crawling peg regime, the authorities fix their currency to one or more foreign currencies but allow it to ease at a regular, pre-set rate.
The issue is already under discussion but will not be settled until next year, he said.
At present the monetary base (M0) is around $1 billion, and total money supply (M2) is about $1.8 billion, the same as gross foreign reserves.
The central bank intervenes in the foreign exchange market but only to smooth fluctuations, not to resist a trend.
"Our general policy is to cut off either seasonal or temporary peaks in demand and supply and keep the exchange rate...from swinging violently," he said.
Dealers said the bank's intervention can be substantial.
In the past two weeks, the tenge currency has been near 70 per dollar and the central bank has not intervened, he said.
Net intervention in 1995 was zero. This year, the central bank is likely to end up a net seller of dollars.
The central bank has so far tended to concentrate its intervention on the Kazakhstan Currency Exchange, where the tenge is fixed in a daily one-hour session.
But volumes on the interbank market are now three to six times greater than on the exchange, Marchenko said.
"Our intervention is shifting to that market, and we will do bilateral deals in that market," he said.
In the longer term, the central bank has to think how to sterilise capital inflows, Marchenko said, noting that investment commitments to Kazakhstan are $46 billion.
Not all of this will come in cash. Oil companies, for instance, are likely to bring in millions of dollars worth of equipment.
"But if it flows in through the foreign exchange market it's a big issue," Marchenko said.
The real problem is likely to arise once portfolio investment and hot money flows into equities.
This is not yet the case as the stock market is poorly developed, and an inadequate infrastructure and regulatory framework are keeping foreign investors away.
"But hopefully, it will be an issue in the second half of next year," he said.

The central bank's tools for sterilisation are fairly limited. It can sell T-bills from its portfolio, which at the moment is relatively small, or can issue its own short-term notes to mop up liquidity. But the short-term notes are a costly instrument.
In summer 1995, the central bank sterilised inflows but also allowed the tenge to appreciate to 54 from 64 per dollar.
The tenge appreciated 30 percent in real terms in 1995, but exports, about 90 percent of which are commodities, grew 54 percent. The real appreciation of the tenge will be much smaller this year.
"The current exchange rate is not hurting commodities," he said, noting there was room for a further small appreciation.
Manufactured goods are in any case uncompetitive because of their quality, he added.
